# The System Design Interview Framework

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Every good system design answer follows the same order: **clarify, estimate, design the API, sketch the architecture, then go deep** on the hardest part. The order matters more than the content.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### The seven steps, in order

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Clarify (ask questions)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Requirements (functional + non-functional)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Estimate scale (back-of-envelope math)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. API design (endpoints in/out)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. High-level design (the skeleton)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Deep dive (the hard part, for real)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
    step_7["7. Scale it further (what breaks first)"]:::step
    step_6 --> step_7
```

#### Functional vs non-functional requirements

| Functional | Non-functional |
| :--- | :--- |
| What the system does: users can post a tweet, follow another user, see a feed | How well it does it: latency, availability, consistency, durability |
| Usually easy to agree on quickly | Where the real design decisions live |
| Drives the API design and data model | Drives the architecture and every trade-off you'll defend |

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Jumping straight to drawing boxes before asking a single clarifying question, which usually means solving a different problem than the one being asked.
- ⚠️ Spending the whole interview on requirements and estimation and never reaching a real deep dive, leaving no evidence of actual engineering judgment.
- ⚠️ Treating every requirement as equally important instead of identifying the one or two that actually constrain the design (e.g. 'must handle 1M writes/sec' constrains far more than 'nice UI').
- ⚠️ ==Presenting a design as if it has no weaknesses==, instead of proactively naming the bottleneck and how you'd address it, which is usually what a strong candidate does unprompted.
- ⚠️ Going deep on a component nobody asked about (like elaborate auth flows) while the actually hard part of the problem (like feed fan-out at scale) gets a single sentence.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why do functional requirements alone not determine a system's architecture?**

> **Model Answer:** Two systems can have identical functional requirements (both let users post and read messages) but need completely different architectures depending on non-functional requirements like scale, latency, and consistency guarantees. A messaging app for 10 friends and a messaging app for 2 billion users do the same 'thing' but are entirely different engineering problems.

**Q: What's the risk of skipping the clarifying-questions step in an interview?**

> **Model Answer:** You risk designing a system that technically works but solves the wrong problem, e.g. designing for strong consistency when the interviewer actually cares about low latency and would accept eventual consistency, or designing for a scale that's off by several orders of magnitude from what was intended.

# Client-Server Architecture & the Request Lifecycle

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Every web request you've ever made is a chain of **translations and handshakes**, name to address, address to connection, connection to encrypted channel, before a single byte of your actual data moves, and each link in that chain is a place a system design can add ==latency or fail==.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### From typing a URL to seeing a page

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. DNS resolution (domain name to IP address)"]:::step
    step_2["2. TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. TLS handshake (cipher agreement, certificate check, shared key)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. HTTP request (method, path, headers, body)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Server processing (route, compute, query)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. HTTP response (status code, headers, body)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
    step_7["7. Render (browser paints the page)"]:::step
    step_6 --> step_7
```

#### The chain of systems behind one request

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client (browser)"]:::client
    dns["DNS Resolver"]:::server
    server["Web Server"]:::server
    db[("Database")]:::db
    client -->|"resolve domain"| dns
    client -->|"TCP + TLS, then HTTP"| server
    server -->|"query"| db
```

#### The request lifecycle as a sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant D as DNS
  participant S as Server
  C->>D: Resolve domain name
  D-->>C: IP address
  C->>S: TCP SYN
  S-->>C: SYN-ACK
  C->>S: ACK
  C->>S: TLS handshake
  C->>S: HTTP request
  S-->>C: HTTP response
```

#### Cost of a new connection vs a reused one

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating 'the request' as a single instantaneous step== instead of a chain of separate network operations, which hides where latency actually comes from.
- ⚠️ Assuming HTTPS only adds encryption, when it also adds real latency from the **TLS handshake**, especially on the first connection before session resumption kicks in.
- ⚠️ ==Designing a client that opens a brand-new connection per request== instead of reusing connections, paying the full DNS+TCP+TLS cost repeatedly for no reason.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that DNS has its own caching and TTL behavior, which means DNS changes (like pointing a domain at a new server) don't take effect everywhere instantly.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does connection reuse matter so much for a system serving many small API requests?**

> **Model Answer:** Each new TCP connection costs a round trip, and each new TLS connection costs one or two more, before any actual data moves. If a client opens a new connection per request, it pays that fixed handshake cost every time, which can dwarf the cost of the actual request. Reusing connections (via keep-alive or HTTP/2 multiplexing) amortizes that cost across many requests instead.

**Q: What does it mean for HTTP to be stateless, and why does that matter for scaling?**

> **Model Answer:** Stateless means the server doesn't retain memory of previous requests from a client, every request must carry whatever context it needs (like an auth token). This matters for scaling because it means any request can be routed to any server behind a load balancer, no request has to go back to the specific server that handled a previous one, which is what makes horizontal scaling with a fleet of interchangeable servers possible in the first place.

# Scalability: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> There are only two ways to serve more load: give one machine more power (**vertical scaling**), or give the work to more machines (**horizontal scaling**), and the second one only works if you first design your system so no machine has to remember anything the others don't.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Vertical vs horizontal scaling

| Vertical (scale up) | Horizontal (scale out) |
| :--- | :--- |
| One machine, more resources (CPU, RAM, disk) | More machines sharing the load |
| Simple, no architecture change needed | Requires statelessness to work at all |
| Hard ceiling: there's a biggest machine you can get | No hard ceiling, keep adding machines |
| Single point of failure remains a single point of failure | One machine dying doesn't take the system down |

#### Stateless servers behind a load balancer

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    s1["App Server 1"]:::server
    s2["App Server 2"]:::server
    s3["App Server 3"]:::server
    cache["Shared Session Store"]:::cache
    client --> lb
    lb --> s1
    lb --> s2
    lb --> s3
    s1 -->|"reads/writes session state"| cache
    s2 -->|"reads/writes session state"| cache
    s3 -->|"reads/writes session state"| cache
```

#### Cost vs capacity: vertical vs horizontal scaling

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming horizontal scaling is always the right answer, when a well-tuned vertical scale is simpler, cheaper, and sufficient for many real systems.
- ⚠️ Adding more servers behind a load balancer without first removing local server state, which causes subtle bugs (like a user randomly getting logged out) instead of the intended capacity increase.
- ⚠️ Treating 'add more servers' as free, ignoring the real added complexity: network calls where there used to be function calls, coordination, and a load balancer that itself needs to be highly available.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that horizontal scaling for a database is a fundamentally harder problem than for a stateless app server, and reaching for sharding before exhausting simpler options like read replicas or vertical scaling.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just add more servers behind a load balancer to scale a system that stores user sessions in server memory?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a session stored in one server's local memory only exists on that server. If the load balancer routes a later request from the same user to a different server, that server has no idea who the user is. Horizontal scaling requires moving that state somewhere shared, like a database or a distributed cache, so any server can serve any request.

**Q: When would vertical scaling actually be the better choice over horizontal scaling?**

> **Model Answer:** When the system is well within the capacity of available hardware, when the workload is genuinely hard to parallelize (like a single-threaded in-memory computation), or when the operational simplicity of one machine outweighs the benefits of elasticity and fault tolerance, common for smaller systems, internal tools, or as a first step before the added complexity of a distributed fleet is actually justified by real load.

# Databases: SQL vs NoSQL

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **SQL** and **NoSQL** aren't 'old vs new' or 'slow vs fast', they're different bets about which is more expensive to give up: strict structure and cross-table consistency, or flexible schema and effortless horizontal scale.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### SQL vs NoSQL

| SQL (relational) | NoSQL |
| :--- | :--- |
| Fixed schema, typed columns, foreign keys | Flexible schema (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) |
| Strong ACID guarantees, safe for transactional data | Built for horizontal scale from the start |
| JOINs make cross-entity queries natural | Consistency across records is usually the app's job |
| Harder to shard while keeping relational guarantees | Great for high-volume, simple-access-pattern data |

#### The four common NoSQL shapes

#### Choosing SQL vs NoSQL by access pattern

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["What's the access pattern?"] --> b{"Need JOINs and strict ACID?"}
  b -->|"Yes"| c["Relational (SQL)"]
  b -->|"No"| d{"Mostly lookup by known key?"}
  d -->|"Yes, huge volume"| e["Key-value / wide-column"]
  d -->|"Flexible, evolving shape"| f["Document store"]
  d -->|"Traversal-heavy"| g["Graph database"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Choosing NoSQL purely because it sounds more scalable, without checking whether the actual access pattern needs relational JOINs and strict consistency.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming a flexible schema means no schema==, when in practice the application still needs a consistent shape, it's just unenforced by the database.
- ⚠️ Believing relational databases can't scale, when in reality read replicas, connection pooling, and even sharding can take a well-designed relational system very far before it becomes the bottleneck.
- ⚠️ Using a single NoSQL database for everything in a system, including data that's deeply relational, instead of considering polyglot persistence for the parts that genuinely need different guarantees.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: A candidate says 'we'll use NoSQL because it's more scalable.' What follow-up question exposes whether they actually understand the trade-off?**

> **Model Answer:** Ask what access pattern the data has: does the system need to join this data against other entities, and does it need strict cross-record consistency? If the answer is yes to either, NoSQL's scalability advantage may come at the cost of pushing hard consistency and relational logic into the application layer, which can be a worse trade than a well-sharded relational database.

**Q: Why might a system use both a relational database and a NoSQL store together?**

> **Model Answer:** Because different parts of the system have different natural access patterns. Core transactional data like orders or account balances benefits from ACID guarantees and JOINs, so it fits relational. A high-volume, simple-lookup use case like session storage or a real-time activity feed benefits from a NoSQL store's horizontal scalability and flexible schema. Using one database per use case (polyglot persistence) is often better than forcing one database to serve both well.

**Q: Why might a system use both a relational database and a NoSQL store together?**

> **Model Answer:** Because different parts of the system have different natural access patterns. Core transactional data like orders or account balances benefits from ACID guarantees and JOINs, so it fits relational. A high-volume, simple-lookup use case like session storage or a real-time activity feed benefits from a NoSQL store's horizontal scalability and flexible schema. Using one database per use case (polyglot persistence) is often better than forcing one database to serve both well.

lesson.content:
# Caching Strategies & Cache Invalidation

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A **cache** only helps if it's usually right and cheap to check, and every caching strategy is really a different answer to one question: when the underlying data changes, how does the cache find out, and what does a reader see in the meantime.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Write-through vs write-back

| Write-through | Write-back |
| :--- | :--- |
| Write goes to cache and database together, synchronously | Write goes to cache immediately, database updated later |
| Cache and database always agree | Writes are fast |
| Every write pays the cost of two systems | Risk of data loss if the cache fails before flushing |

#### Cache-aside on a read

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Check cache (is the data there?)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Cache miss (not found or expired)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Read from database (the source of truth)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Write result into cache (for next time)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Return to caller (future reads hit the cache)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Cache hit rate vs. cache size (working set = 10,000 hot items)

#### Cache stampede: locked refill vs. unprotected refill

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant R1 as Request 1
  participant R2 as Request 2..N
  participant C as Cache
  participant D as Database
  R1->>C: read (miss, expired)
  R1->>C: acquire refill lock
  R2->>C: read (miss too)
  C-->>R2: wait, refill in progress
  R1->>D: single query to refill
  D-->>R1: fresh value
  R1->>C: write value, release lock
  C-->>R2: serve fresh cached value
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Adding a cache without a real invalidation plan, treating 'it'll expire eventually' as sufficient for data where staleness actually matters.
- ⚠️ Using a TTL so long that users see meaningfully outdated data, or so short that the cache barely reduces database load at all, without deliberately choosing the trade-off.
- ⚠️ Not accounting for cache stampede, letting a single hot key's expiration cause a burst of simultaneous database load right when the system can least afford it.
- ⚠️ Caching data that changes on nearly every read, adding cache complexity and a consistency risk for a hit rate that's barely better than not caching at all.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a cache is a second copy of the truth, and every code path that writes the underlying data needs to also handle the cache, not just the 'main' write path.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is cache invalidation considered a genuinely hard problem instead of just an implementation detail?**

> **Model Answer:** Because it requires knowing, at the moment underlying data changes, every cached representation of that data that now needs to be updated or removed, across potentially many cache keys, layers, and services, while concurrent reads and writes keep happening. Getting this wrong doesn't crash the system, it silently serves incorrect data, which is often worse than an outage because nobody notices immediately.

**Q: When would you choose write-back over write-through for a cache?**

> **Model Answer:** When write latency matters more than the small risk of data loss, for example a high-throughput analytics counter or a system where losing the last few milliseconds of writes on a rare cache failure is acceptable. Write-through is preferred when correctness on every write matters more than raw write speed, like anything touching financial balances.

lesson.content:
# Consistency Models & the CAP Theorem

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The **CAP theorem** isn't a menu you pick freely from, network partitions will happen whether you plan for them or not, so the real choice every distributed system makes is what happens during one: keep answering and risk being wrong, or refuse to answer until you can be sure.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### CP vs AP during a network partition

| CP (consistency over availability) | AP (availability over consistency) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Refuses or delays requests during a partition | Keeps answering using local data during a partition |
| Guarantees no stale or conflicting reads | May return stale data temporarily, reconciled later |
| Right fit: banking, inventory, anything where wrong is worse than slow | Right fit: social feeds, like counts, presence indicators |

#### CAP as a triangle of trade-offs

#### What a node does when a partition happens

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  p["Network partition detected"] --> ask{"Is being wrong worse than being unavailable?"}
  ask -->|"yes, e.g. a ledger"| cp["Choose CP: refuse or error"]
  ask -->|"no, e.g. a like count"| ap["Choose AP: answer with local data"]
  cp --> cpresult["No stale reads, some requests fail"]
  ap --> apresult["Always answers, may be briefly stale"]
  apresult --> reconcile["Reconcile once partition heals"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Claiming a system 'chooses CA', treating partition tolerance as optional, when any real distributed system will eventually face a partition and has to have a defined behavior for it.
- ⚠️ Assuming eventual consistency means 'basically the same as strong consistency, just a little slower', when the actual guarantee (convergence only if writes stop) can allow meaningfully stale or conflicting reads under continuous load.
- ⚠️ Applying the same consistency model to an entire system, when different pieces of data (financial balance vs. like count) usually deserve different points on the consistency spectrum.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that CAP is specifically about partition-time behavior, and using it to argue about normal-operation latency trade-offs, which is really what PACELC is about.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is it inaccurate to say a system 'chooses CA' in the CAP theorem?**

> **Model Answer:** Because partition tolerance isn't a feature you can opt out of, network partitions are a real, unavoidable failure mode in any system with more than one node communicating over a network. 'Choosing CA' would mean assuming partitions never happen, which isn't realistic. The actual choice a system makes is what to do when a partition does happen: stay consistent by refusing some requests (CP), or stay available by answering with possibly stale data (AP).

**Q: Give an example of a real feature where you'd deliberately choose AP over CP, and explain why.**

> **Model Answer:** A 'likes' counter on a social media post. During a network partition, it's far better for the system to keep accepting and displaying likes, even if the count is briefly slightly off between replicas, than to stop the feature from working entirely. The cost of being briefly wrong (an undercount or overcount by a few) is much lower than the cost of the feature being unavailable, which makes AP the right choice here.

# Database Replication & Sharding

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Replication** copies the same data onto more machines so more people can read it at once and it survives a failure; **sharding** splits different data across more machines so more data can be written and stored at once, and most large systems eventually need both, for different reasons.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Leader-follower replication with read replicas

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    leader[("Leader DB")]:::db
    r1[("Follower 1")]:::db
    r2[("Follower 2")]:::db
    app -->|"writes"| leader
    leader -.->|"replicate"| r1
    leader -.->|"replicate"| r2
    app -->|"reads"| r1
    app -->|"reads"| r2
```

#### Hash-based sharding across three shards

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    router["Shard Router (hash of user ID)"]:::server
    s1[("Shard 1 (users hash 0)")]:::db
    s2[("Shard 2 (users hash 1)")]:::db
    s3[("Shard 3 (users hash 2)")]:::db
    app --> router
    router --> s1
    router --> s2
    router --> s3
```

#### Which scaling problem do I actually have?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["Database is struggling"] --> b{"Reads or writes/storage?"}
  b -->|"Too many reads"| c["Add read replicas (replication)"]
  b -->|"Too much data or writes"| d["Split data across shards"]
  d --> e{"Is shard key even?"}
  e -->|"Yes"| f["Load spreads evenly"]
  e -->|"No"| g["Hot shard bottleneck"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming replication alone solves write scaling, when ==only the leader accepts writes== in a standard leader-follower setup, replicas don't add write capacity.
- ⚠️ Reading from a replica and expecting to immediately see a write that was just made to the leader, without accounting for **replication lag**.
- ⚠️ Choosing a shard key based on convenience (like an auto-incrementing ID) rather than actual access and traffic patterns, creating ==hot shards== down the line.
- ⚠️ Underestimating how hard cross-shard queries and transactions become, and sharding before exhausting simpler options like vertical scaling or read replicas.
- ⚠️ Treating sharding as purely a technical decision, when rebalancing shards later (as data grows unevenly) is a genuinely difficult migration that's much easier to plan for upfront than retrofit.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't adding more read replicas help a write-heavy workload?**

> **Model Answer:** In a standard leader-follower setup, only the leader accepts writes, followers just replicate what the leader already wrote. Adding more followers increases read capacity and redundancy, but every write still has to go through the single leader, so write throughput is bounded by what one machine can handle. Scaling writes requires sharding (splitting the data itself across multiple leaders) rather than more replicas of the same leader.

**Q: What makes choosing a shard key the single most important decision in a sharding scheme?**

> **Model Answer:** Because it determines whether load is actually distributed evenly across shards. A shard key that clusters real-world traffic unevenly, like sharding by customer when one customer accounts for a huge share of activity, creates a hot shard that becomes the new bottleneck no matter how many total shards exist. A good shard key also affects how expensive range queries and rebalancing will be later, and it's very difficult to change once a system has real data and traffic on it.

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**

**Q: Why do consumers reading from a queue need to be idempotent even if the queue technology claims reliable delivery?**

> **Model Answer:** Because most real-world delivery guarantees are at-least-once, not exactly-once. A consumer can crash after processing a message but before acknowledging it, causing the queue to redeliver that same message. If processing isn't idempotent, that redelivery could cause duplicate side effects, like charging a customer twice or sending the same notification twice, so the consumer itself needs to detect and safely handle duplicate messages.

**Q: What's the risk of putting a task on a queue with no backpressure policy?**

> **Model Answer:** If producers keep publishing faster than consumers can process, and there's no defined response, like slowing producers, autoscaling consumers, or shedding lower-priority messages, the queue just grows unbounded. That eventually exhausts memory or storage on the queue itself, turning a temporary processing lag into a hard outage, and it also means the eventual backlog might be so large that by the time it's processed, the work is stale or no longer useful.

# API Design: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **REST**, **GraphQL**, and **gRPC** are not competing on quality, they're built for different shapes of problem: resources you fetch and mutate, flexible queries across a graph of data, and fast typed calls between internal services. Picking one is really picking which caller you're optimizing for.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### REST vs GraphQL: fetching a user's profile with their last 3 posts

| REST | GraphQL |
| :--- | :--- |
| GET /users/42 returns the user | One query asks for user { name, posts(limit: 3) { title } } |
| GET /users/42/posts?limit=3 returns the posts, a second round trip | One round trip returns exactly those fields, nothing more |
| Response shape is fixed by the server, client takes what it's given | Server resolves the nested relationship internally |

#### Where each style typically sits in one system

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    mobile["Mobile app"]:::client
    web["Web app"]:::client
    gateway["GraphQL gateway"]:::server
    userservice["User service"]:::server
    postservice["Post service"]:::server
    partner["Partner integration"]:::client
    restapi["Public REST API"]:::server
    mobile -->|"GraphQL query"| gateway
    web -->|"GraphQL query"| gateway
    gateway -->|"gRPC call"| userservice
    gateway -->|"gRPC call"| postservice
    partner -->|"HTTP GET/POST"| restapi
```

#### Which API style fits your caller?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  start["Who is calling this API?"] --> internal{"Internal service you control?"}
  internal -->|"yes"| grpc["gRPC: fast, typed, binary"]
  internal -->|"no"| shapes{"Do client shapes vary a lot?"}
  shapes -->|"yes, many apps/screens"| graphql["GraphQL: client picks fields"]
  shapes -->|"no, fixed resources"| rest["REST: cacheable, universal"]
```

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Treating this as a single 'best API style' debate instead of matching the style to who is calling the API and how often the required data shape changes.
- ⚠️ Adopting GraphQL without building query depth limits or cost analysis, leaving the server open to a single expensive nested query taking down the database.
- ⚠️ Using gRPC for a public-facing API that third-party developers or browsers need to call directly, ignoring that most browsers and casual integrators can't easily consume it.
- ⚠️ Designing a REST API with dozens of screen-specific endpoints to work around fixed response shapes, when that pain is exactly the signal that GraphQL might fit better.
- ⚠️ Assuming GraphQL is automatically faster than REST, when a poorly resolved GraphQL query can be far slower than a well-cached REST endpoint for the same data.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't GraphQL simply replace REST everywhere, given that it removes over-fetching and under-fetching?**

> **Model Answer:** GraphQL trades those wins for real costs: a single flexible endpoint is harder to cache with standard HTTP caching, harder to rate-limit sensibly since queries vary in cost, and requires server-side protections against expensive nested queries that a fixed-shape REST endpoint never needs. For simple, cacheable, widely-consumed public APIs, REST's constraints are often a feature, not a limitation.

**Q: Why is gRPC a poor fit for a public API that any third-party developer might call?**

> **Model Answer:** gRPC requires the client to have the same .proto schema compiled in, isn't natively callable from a browser without a proxying layer, and produces binary payloads that are hard to inspect with generic tools like curl or a browser's network tab. Public APIs prioritize broad compatibility and easy debugging by unknown developers, which is exactly what REST's plain-text, universally-supported HTTP model provides.

**Q: What's a concrete example of the N+1 problem in GraphQL, and how is it typically fixed?**

> **Model Answer:** A query asking for 50 posts, each with its author, can naively trigger 1 query for the posts plus 50 separate queries, one per post, to fetch each author. It's typically fixed with a batching layer like DataLoader, which collects all the author IDs requested during one tick and issues a single batched query for all of them instead of one query per item.

# Rate Limiting

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> **Rate limiting** caps how often a client can call your system in a given window, and the algorithm you pick decides how forgiving that cap is about bursts, not just what the average rate ends up being.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Token bucket vs leaky bucket

| Token bucket | Leaky bucket |
| :--- | :--- |
| Tokens refill at a steady rate, up to a max bucket size | Requests queue and are processed at a constant output rate |
| Allows bursts up to the bucket capacity | Smooths bursts into steady, predictable downstream load |
| Rejects a request outright once tokens run out | Queued requests wait, adding latency during a burst |

#### A layered rate limiter in front of an API

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    cdn["CDN / edge"]:::server
    gateway["API gateway (rate limiter)"]:::server
    store["Redis (counters/tokens)"]:::cache
    server["App server"]:::server
    client -->|"request"| cdn
    cdn -->|"coarse limit passed"| gateway
    gateway -->|"check/update count"| store
    gateway -->|"allowed request"| server
```

#### Token bucket, per request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  req["Request arrives"] --> check{"Token available?"}
  check -->|"yes"| consume["Consume token, allow request"]
  check -->|"no"| reject["Reject: 429 + Retry-After"]
  consume --> refill["Bucket refills over time"]
  reject --> refill
```

#### Fixed window's boundary burst vs sliding window

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Implementing a naive fixed window counter== without realizing it allows nearly double the intended rate right at the window boundary.
- ⚠️ Rate limiting only by **IP address**, which unfairly throttles many legitimate users sharing a NAT or corporate gateway while barely slowing down a distributed attacker.
- ⚠️ Enforcing the limit locally per server instance in a multi-server deployment, letting a client's effective limit multiply by however many servers happen to receive its requests.
- ⚠️ Returning a bare rejection with no Retry-After or remaining-quota information, leaving well-behaved clients to retry blindly instead of backing off correctly.
- ⚠️ Setting one blanket limit for every endpoint, instead of tighter limits on expensive operations (like search or file upload) and looser ones on cheap operations (like a health check).

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a fixed window counter allow more than the stated limit in practice, and how does sliding window fix it?**

> **Model Answer:** A fixed window resets sharply at each boundary, so a client can send the full limit in the last moment of one window and the full limit again in the first moment of the next, achieving nearly double the intended rate in a short span around the boundary. A sliding window avoids this by never having a hard reset point, either tracking exact timestamps or smoothly weighting between the current and previous window, so no short span of time ever sees more than the intended limit.

**Q: Why is per-IP rate limiting often insufficient on its own?**

> **Model Answer:** Many real, distinct users can share one IP address behind a NAT, corporate network, or mobile carrier gateway, so limiting by IP alone can throttle legitimate unrelated users together as if they were one client. Conversely, a determined attacker can spread requests across many IPs to evade the limit entirely. Combining IP-based limits with per-account or per-API-key limits gives more accurate, fairer enforcement.

**Q: In a system with many API server instances behind a load balancer, why can't each server just enforce the rate limit independently?**

> **Model Answer:** If each server keeps its own local count, a client's requests get distributed across servers by the load balancer, and each server only sees a fraction of that client's total traffic, undercounting it. The client's effective allowed rate becomes the per-server limit multiplied by however many servers it happens to hit, defeating the intended cap. A shared store like Redis, tracked centrally, is needed to enforce one true limit across the whole fleet.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

```mermaid

**Q: Why does a CDN help almost nothing for a personalized dashboard endpoint, even if the endpoint is popular?**

> **Model Answer:** Caching only helps when many requests can be served the same cached response. > **Model Answer:** Origin pull requires no upfront work but means the first request for any piece of content in a given region pays full origin latency before it's cached. # Microservices vs Monolith

> **Difficulty:** `INTERMEDIATE` | **Target Companies:** `FAANG / Top Tech` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The real trade-off isn't old versus modern, it's whether you need **independent deployment** and team boundaries badly enough to pay for it in ==operational complexity== and turning what used to be a function call into a network call.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Monolith vs microservices

| Monolith | Microservices |
| :--- | :--- |
| One codebase, one deployment, in-process function calls | Independently deployable services, each often owning its own data |
| Transactions can span the whole system atomically | Function calls become network calls, needing retries and timeouts |
| Simple to run, but releases and teams are coupled together | Teams deploy and scale independently, at the cost of real operational overhead |

#### The same feature, one function call vs several network calls

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client request"]:::client
    mono["Monolith (checkout module)"]:::server
    monodb[("Single database")]:::db
    orders["Order service"]:::server
    payments["Payment service"]:::server
    inventory["Inventory service"]:::server
    client -->|"checkout"| mono
    mono -->|"one atomic transaction"| monodb
    client -->|"checkout"| orders
    orders -->|"network call"| payments
    orders -->|"network call"| inventory
```

#### Deciding whether to actually split a service out

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  start["Considering microservices?"] --> pain{"Real deploy or scaling pain today?"}
  pain -->|"no"| stay["Stay monolith (or modular monolith)"]
  pain -->|"yes"| tooling{"Have service discovery and tracing?"}
  tooling -->|"no"| build["Build that tooling first"]
  tooling -->|"yes"| split["Split out the specific bottleneck"]
```

#### Coordination cost vs team size (illustrative model)

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Adopting microservices because they're seen as modern or resume-worthy==, without a real organizational or scaling pain that a monolith was actually causing.
- ⚠️ Underestimating how much harder data consistency becomes once each service owns its own database, and only discovering the need for sagas or eventual consistency after a production bug.
- ⚠️ Splitting a system into services along the wrong boundaries, so that most features still need to touch three or four services together, keeping the coordination cost of a monolith while adding the network cost of microservices on top.
- ⚠️ Ignoring the operational prerequisites, service discovery, monitoring, distributed tracing, and jumping to microservices before the team has the tooling maturity to run them reliably.
- ⚠️ Treating the decision as permanent and binary, instead of recognizing a modular monolith can evolve into microservices later, once real scaling or team-coordination pain actually shows up.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is 'microservices are more scalable' an incomplete answer in an interview?**

> **Model Answer:** A monolith can scale horizontally too, by running many identical copies behind a load balancer, as long as it's stateless. What microservices actually add is the ability to scale different components independently and at different rates, a payment service handling 10x the load of a recommendation service can get 10x the instances without over-provisioning the rest of the system. The scaling win is about independence and granularity, not raw capability that a monolith categorically lacks.

**Q: What specifically breaks when a multi-step operation that used to be one database transaction is split across microservices?**

> **Model Answer:** A monolith can wrap several writes in a single atomic transaction, so either all of them succeed or none do, with the database enforcing that guarantee. Split across services with separate databases, there's no single transaction spanning all of them, so a partial failure (step one succeeds, step two fails) can leave the system in an inconsistent state unless it's explicitly handled with a pattern like a saga, which runs compensating actions to undo the completed steps if a later step fails.

**Q: When would you actively recommend staying with a monolith over splitting into microservices?**

> **Model Answer:** When there's a single team, or a small number of tightly coordinated teams, working on the system, when the team lacks the operational tooling (service discovery, distributed tracing, per-service deployment pipelines) to run many services reliably, or when no specific component actually needs to scale or deploy independently from the rest yet. In those cases, microservices add real network and consistency costs without a corresponding organizational or scaling benefit to justify them.
